findings.title: Ingest accepts writes from anyone, with no authentication
findings.description: The handler advertises an `authorization` header in its CORS allow-list but never reads or validates one, and `access-control-allow-origin: *` invites any page to POST. Anyone who learns the deployment URL can write unlimited reviews into the team's blob store — fabricating developer names, commit messages and finding counts, and driving storage cost — and the content they inject is rendered directly on the dashboard. The extension already threads `CR_TRACK_INGEST_TOKEN` through `deliver()`, so the sending half of a shared-secret check exists; only the verifying half is missing.
findings.suggestion: Consider verifying a bearer token (e.g. from an `INGEST_TOKEN` env var) against the `authorization` header before `save()`, returning 401 when it does not match, and narrowing the allow-origin to the dashboard's own origin.

findings.title: taskkill spawn failure escapes the try/catch and can crash the host
findings.description: `spawn` reports a missing or unrunnable executable asynchronously via an `error` event, not by throwing, so the surrounding `try/catch` never sees it. This ChildProcess has no `error` listener, and Node rethrows an unhandled `error` event as an uncaught exception — from `killAllChildren()` during `deactivate`, or from the timeout path in `run()`. On a Windows box where `taskkill` is not on PATH (locked-down images, a trimmed System32 PATH), every kill attempt would take the extension host down, and the portable SIGTERM fallback is never reached because the function has already returned.
findings.suggestion: Consider attaching an `error` listener to the taskkill child that falls back to the portable kill path, so a missing taskkill degrades instead of throwing.

findings.title: Full reports are stored as public blobs with predictable-ish names and a one-year cache
findings.description: `access: "public"` with `addRandomSuffix: false` means every blob is fetchable directly from the blob CDN, bypassing the API entirely — so any access control added to `api/review.js` later can be walked around by anyone who has seen a blob URL. Keys are `<ISO timestamp>__<client-supplied id>`, and since ingest is unauthenticated an attacker can choose their own `review.id`, making the namespace partly guessable. The one-year `cacheControlMaxAge` also means a report cannot be effectively withdrawn once a URL has leaked.
findings.suggestion: Consider switching these to private blobs read through the API with a short-lived signed URL, or at minimum re-enabling `addRandomSuffix` so a URL cannot be guessed from a key.

findings.title: Newest-first listing breaks once the index exceeds 1000 blobs
findings.description: `list()` is capped at 1000 and returns pathnames in ascending lexicographic order, and the keys begin with an ISO timestamp — so once there are more than 1000 index blobs, the page returns the *oldest* 1000 and the client-side descending sort only reorders that stale slice. The dashboard would then stop showing new reviews entirely, with no error to explain it. Given nothing ever prunes `index/`, a busy team reaches this quietly.
findings.suggestion: Consider paginating with the cursor `list()` returns until exhausted (or reversing the key so the newest sorts first, e.g. an inverted timestamp prefix) so recency does not depend on staying under the page cap.

findings.title: Every page load fans out to 200 blob fetches, and the page polls every 15s
findings.description: `recent()` issues one `fetch` per index blob — up to 200 — on each `/api/reviews` request, and `public/index.html` calls `load()` on a 15-second interval per open tab. That is ~800 blob reads per minute per viewer against a serverless function with a request timeout, and it grows linearly with review count. `renderRows()` also rebuilds `tbody.innerHTML` on every poll, clearing each detail box's `dataset.loaded`, so every expanded row re-fetches its full report on the same cadence.
findings.suggestion: Consider keeping enough in the index blob's own metadata to skip the per-blob fetch, or caching the assembled list briefly server-side; and on the client, skipping the re-render when the returned key set is unchanged.

findings.title: Request body is read into memory with no size limit
findings.description: The manual body path accumulates chunks until the stream ends, with no cap, and `JSON.stringify` of the result is then written to blob storage. Combined with the unauthenticated endpoint, a single large POST can exhaust the function's memory or write an arbitrarily large blob. Reports do legitimately vary in size, so the limit wants to be generous rather than absent.
findings.suggestion: Consider tracking the accumulated byte count and responding 413 past a generous ceiling (a few MB), which also keeps a runaway extension from filling the store.

findings.title: Review metadata is world-readable, including developer emails and commit messages
findings.description: `GET /api/reviews` has no authentication and a wildcard allow-origin, so anyone with the URL gets every developer's name and email address, repository and branch names, commit SHAs and commit messages for the whole team. `GET /api/review?key=…` then returns the full report for any of those keys, which carries the finding text and any diff excerpts the review captured. That combination is a fairly complete picture of a private codebase and its contributors.
findings.suggestion: Consider putting the read endpoints behind the same shared secret or a Vercel deployment protection / SSO layer, and restricting the allow-origin to the dashboard itself.

findings.title: Deploy uploads every file in the directory, including any local .env
findings.description: `SKIP` excludes `node_modules`, `.vercel`, `.git` and `deploy.js`, but nothing else — so a `.env`, `.env.local`, or any credential file a developer leaves in `dashboard/` is read and shipped as a deployment file. Reading with `"utf8"` also means any binary asset added later (an image, a font) is silently corrupted rather than rejected.
findings.suggestion: Consider skipping dotfiles by default (or at least `.env*`) and either base64-encoding non-text files or failing loudly on them.

findings.title: Renamed files parse into a bogus path, which can silently drop the whole review
findings.description: With rename detection on (git's default since 2.9), `git show --numstat` writes a rename as a single combined path — `src/{old => new}.ts` — rather than two tab-separated names. `rest[rest.length - 1]` therefore captures that brace form, which never matches the plain new path that `--name-status` puts in `typeByPath`, so `changeType` falls back to "modified" and `languageFor` sees an extension it may not recognise. Worse, `extension.ts` feeds these paths straight to `commitDiff` as a pathspec; git does not expand braces in pathspecs, so a rename-only commit yields an empty diff and is skipped with "produced an empty diff", and a mixed commit reviews only the non-renamed files.
findings.suggestion: Consider running numstat with `-z` (where renames come back as three NUL-separated fields) or passing `--no-renames`, so the path recorded is a real pathspec.

findings.title: A commit made during a review is dropped permanently, not queued
findings.description: `CommitWatcher.check()` advances `lastSeen` as soon as it observes a new SHA, independently of whether the review actually ran. If a second commit lands while the first review is still in flight — an `--amend`, a quick follow-up fix, or a rebase-free two-commit push — `reviewCommit` returns early and that SHA is never revisited, since the watcher now considers it seen. The developer gets one log line and no review for a commit that arguably needed one most.
findings.suggestion: Consider holding the most recent pending SHA in a field and reviewing it once the in-flight run finishes, so a superseding commit is deferred rather than discarded.

findings.title: Deploy poll ignores a failed status request
findings.description: `poll.ok` is never checked, so a transient 429 or 500 from the Vercel API yields a body without `readyState`/`status`; `state` becomes `undefined`, the loop keeps spinning until the five-minute deadline, and the script exits 1 reporting `Final state: undefined` for what may well be a healthy deployment.
findings.suggestion: Consider keeping the previous `state` when a poll response is not ok, and treating repeated poll failures as a distinct, named outcome.
